title: The shortest great sutra
hookLine: a few lines on the perfection of wisdom, chanted daily across East Asia and Tibet; read in Müller's 1894 translation

lines: A WHOLE TEACHING ON ONE PAGE.
cards: A whole teaching on wisdom, on a single page. It's short enough to chant before a kettle boils, yet in that space it tries to say what wisdom sees, and it ends with a few syllables meant to be said out loud.
Monks chant it from memory; so do lay people at home altars. For the next ten days, this path reads it slowly, line by line. Today's word: prajnaparamita, the perfection of wisdom.

teach.h: THE HEART OF THE PERFECTION OF WISDOM.
teach.b: Its full name is the Heart of the Perfection of Wisdom Sutra, usually just called the Heart Sutra.
It belongs to the Mahayana, the branch of Buddhism found across East Asia, Tibet, Mongolia and Vietnam.
Theravada Buddhists, whose Pali texts filled these past weeks, don't use it as scripture; it comes from a different family of texts, and both families are honored by their own communities.
Prajnaparamita is two Sanskrit words. Prajna is wisdom, the deep seeing that understands how things really are.
Paramita is perfection, but there's a well-known traditional reading of it: para, the far shore, and ita, gone.
Wisdom gone beyond. Wisdom that has crossed over. Some modern scholars trace the word instead to parama, the highest.
But the image of crossing has stuck, and the text itself will use it. There's a whole library of perfection-of-wisdom texts, some of them enormous; one is even named for its hundred thousand lines.
The Heart Sutra is their heart: the whole teaching pressed into a page. There's also an English connection.
In the eighteen eighties, Max Müller in Oxford, working with the Japanese scholar Bunyiu Nanjio, published the Sanskrit text from old palm leaves kept at the temple of Horyuji in Japan.
Müller's English translation appeared in eighteen ninety-four, and it's freely available. So it's a short text, with a very long reach.

how: The Heart Sutra is chanted daily in many Zen, Chan, Korean Seon and Tibetan communities, often at morning and evening services; Theravada communities do not use it as scripture.

games.q: you're a Buddhist in Sri Lanka and a friend from Japan asks if you chant the Heart Sutra every morning. what's the likeliest answer?
o: probably not: it's a Mahayana text, and Theravada communities chant Pali texts instead.
games.why: the Heart Sutra belongs to the Mahayana family; Theravada communities honor their own Pali texts. neither is ranked here.

practice: Rest with the breath for a moment, and hold one phrase lightly: wisdom gone beyond. Picture a wide river, and the far shore on the other side. Don't try to cross; just know the shore is there.
